nodes.title: Minkowski’s sharp upper product inequality
nodes.statement: For a discrete full Z-lattice L in a finite-dimensional real inner-product space E and a centrally symmetric convex body K with 0 in its interior, (∏_{i:Fin d}λ_i(L,K))·volume.real(K)≤2^d·covolume(L), where d=dim_R E and λ_i is the inherited zero-based successive minimum. The formula includes d=0.
hypotheses: E carries its native Borel structure and canonical intrinsic Euclidean volume. L uses native Submodule Z E, DiscreteTopology and IsZLattice. K uses native ConvexBody. The inherited real-valued gauge minimum interface is a plan, not a new completed library implementation.
Lower-rank lattices are first regarded as full lattices in their real spans, with intrinsic measure. No ambient-volume conclusion for a lower-dimensional body is substituted.
proofSteps: Choose an integral basis b adapted to the strict minimum flag by integral-minimum-flag; its real extension is native b.ofZLatticeBasis. This need not be the attained minimum family.
Let e=(b.ofZLatticeBasis).equivFunL and K'=e(K), using the native compact convex image. Continuity, bijectivity and linearity preserve the zero-interior and central-symmetry hypotheses.

For z∈Z^d take x=b.equivFun⁻¹(z)∈L. Native ofZLatticeBasis_repr_apply identifies e(x)=c(z), and gauge-linear-equiv identifies its gauge. Native mem_flag_iff_repr_eq_zero turns the inherited strict flag into the coordinate-flag hypothesis for a_i=λ_i. Native coordinate/basis bijectivity supplies every integer vector, not just an inclusion of a sublattice.
Use successive-minimum-pos and successive-minimum-monotone, then coordinate-flag-upper to obtain (∏λ_i)volume.real(K')≤2^d.

Import native ZLattice.volume_image_eq_volume_div_covolume' for the compact measurable K: volume(K')=volume(K)/ofReal(covolume(L)). Covolume positivity and finite compact volume permit real conversion and multiplication by covolume(L), giving the displayed inequality with exactly that factor.

The coordinate theorem includes d=0, so the empty basis/product and one-point volume discharge that case without selecting a nonexistent first or last minimum. No minimum-normalization assumption λ_0≥1 is introduced.
acceptance: For L=2Z and K=[−3,3], minimum 2/3 times length 6 is 4=2·covolume(L); omitting covolume would assert 4≤2.
For L=2Z×3Z and K=[−2,2]×[−1,1], minima (1,3) and area 8 give 24=4·6.
In the zero-dimensional canonical space the empty product, volume, covolume and 2^0 are all one.

nodes.title: Integral quadratic lattices over a Dedekind domain
nodes.statement: For a Dedekind domain R with fraction field K, a finite-dimensional K-space V and native q:V→K quadratic, an integral quadratic lattice is L:Submodule R V with Submodule.IsLattice K L and q(L)⊆R. Nondegeneracy of q and unimodularity of its integral polar pairing are separate predicates. There is no global free-basis field.
hypotheses: K has characteristic different from 2 for the field-classification interface; the native integral quadratic-map definition itself does not require 2 to be a unit in R.
The embedding R→K and scalar tower are fixed. Invariant-factor and genus work uses a nondegenerate generic fibre.
proofSteps: Bundle the existing submodule and IsLattice certificate with the existing QuadraticForm and the exact image-in-R condition.
Restrict q to L using injectivity of R→K; obtain a native R-valued QuadraticMap.
Compare the rational symmetric bilinear carrier with completed IntegralLattices only under its stated integrality/evenness convention; do not replace q by half a bilinear diagonal over a dyadic ring.
acceptance: R=Z, K=Q, L=Z and q(x)=x² give an integral lattice whose polar pairing is 2xy and is not unimodular.
The integral symmetric pairing B(x,y)=xy on Z does not make q(x)=B(x,x)/2 integral.
A nonprincipal fractional ideal is allowed as an R-lattice; no constructor asks for an R-basis.

nodes.title: Integral genus inside a rational quadratic space
nodes.statement: Within a fixed nondegenerate quadratic K-space (V,q), two integral R-lattices belong to the same genus when their completed lattices are isometric under O(q_v)(K_v) at every nonzero prime v. If quadratic spaces themselves vary, also require the archimedean signature data and the rational-space identification from GlobalQuadraticForms. Genus classes are integral isometry classes inside this equivalence class.
hypotheses: R is the ring of integers of a number field, or a specified localization with exactly its retained places.
Genus, rational isometry and global integral isometry have separate types and separate quotient relations.
proofSteps: Use completed-lattice scalar change and the imported local orthogonal groups.
Prove reflexivity, symmetry and transitivity by composing local isometries.
Take the setoid quotient by global integral isometry inside the genus; do not quotient by unrelated local choices.
IntegralLattices Layer 4 owns the Z/Q class, genus and proper-spinor-genus specialization. Import it and compare the number-field/Dedekind extension; keep its rank-specific class-count restrictions.

nodes.title: Proper spinor genus
nodes.statement: For nondegenerate q in characteristic different from 2, proper spinor genus is the orbit of an integral lattice under SO(q)(K) times the image of Spin(q)(A_f)→SO(q)(A_f), acting on its finite adelic completion. Proper genus uses SO instead of O. Their forgetful maps to ordinary genus are separate.
hypotheses: Use the actual local-field image of the spin covering; no blanket surjectivity on local rational points.
Dyadic spinor-norm images and signatures are supplied by their owners or left as precise gaps.
proofSteps: Import the general-field spin covering and spinor norm from OrthogonalSpinGroups Layer 1 and its adelic specialization from Layer 3; use AdelicAlgebraicGroups only for additional general number-field/group functoriality.
Define the orbit relation from those actual groups and prove equivalence by group laws.
The spin image is contained in SO, so construct maps to proper genus and ordinary genus.
The adelic/local integral stabilizer and spinor-norm comparison proof is still a recorded input.
IntegralLattices Layer 4 owns the Z/Q class, genus and proper-spinor-genus specialization. Import it and compare the number-field/Dedekind extension; keep its rank-specific class-count restrictions.
acceptance: At a place where a nontrivial spinor-norm class occurs, an SO-point with that norm cannot be inserted into the spin image merely by asserting surjectivity.
A proper spinor-genus relation implies genus; the converse is not an API lemma.
For rank one the proper orthogonal group is trivial; no higher-rank spin-image claim is inferred from that case.

nodes.title: Integral hermitian lattices
nodes.statement: Let K be a field with involution, R⊂K a stable integral subring and V a finite K-space. A hermitian integral lattice consists of native L:Submodule R V, Submodule.IsLattice K L and a native sesquilinear H, conjugate-linear in its first argument and linear in its second, with H(y,x)=star H(x,y) and H(L,L)⊆R. Generic nondegeneracy is distinct from integral self-duality.
hypotheses: Commutative K/R in this declaration; the quaternionic right-module variant is a separate target.
For Li–Zhang density the extension is unramified quadratic F/F₀ and F₀ has characteristic different from 2; dyadic residue fields are allowed in §3 except its explicitly geometric branch.
proofSteps: Reuse Submodule.IsLattice and the pinned star-sesquilinear form rather than introducing a new bilinear carrier.
Bundle the actual symmetry and integral image conditions.
Transport along a K-linear isometry carrying the R-lattice onto the target; retain the coefficient involution.
acceptance: For rank one over an unramified quadratic extension, H(x,y)=star(x)y on O_F is integral and self-dual.
Replacing conjugate transpose by ordinary transpose on the complex vector (i) changes its Gram value from 1 to −1.
An integral hermitian lattice with nonunit Gram determinant is nondegenerate over F but not self-dual over O_F.

nodes.title: Hermitian dual lattice
nodes.statement: For a nondegenerate integral hermitian lattice L in V, define L∨={x∈V : H(x,L)⊆R}; under the stable involution this equals the right-dual condition H(L,x)⊆R. This is a full finite R-lattice over a Dedekind domain; integrality is equivalent to L⊆L∨. Self-duality means equality, not just equality of generic spans.
hypotheses: R is Dedekind and stable under the involution; H is nondegenerate on the generic fibre.
No finiteness of residue fields is needed until cardinalities are used.
proofSteps: Show the defining set is an R-submodule using sesquilinearity and stability of R under star.
Use a local free basis to express the dual by the inverse hermitian Gram matrix; descend the finite lattice property.
Use symmetry to compare the two pairing directions and prove the inclusion characterization.
Local inverse-Gram and descent adapters remain explicit proof gaps.
acceptance: For rank-one Gram π^a over an unramified extension, the dual of O_F e is π^−a O_F e.
The Gram-1 lattice is self-dual; Gram-π lattice is integral but not self-dual.
The zero-dimensional lattice equals its dual and has zero discriminant length.

nodes.title: Fundamental invariants of a local hermitian lattice
nodes.statement: For an integral nondegenerate O_F-hermitian lattice L of rank n over a DVR, attach the unique ordered a₁≤…≤a_n with a_i≥0 and L∨/L≅⊕O_F/π^{a_i}; define val(L)=Σa_i and t(L)=#{i:a_i>0}. Vertex means a_i∈{0,1}; self-dual means all a_i=0.
hypotheses: The quotient is measured by O_F-length; q is the size of the residue field of F₀ when F/F₀ is unramified quadratic.
A_i=0 contributes the zero summand; n=0 has length/type 0.
proofSteps: Apply imported Smith normal form locally to the inclusion L→L∨; do not plan Smith normal form again.
Read off ordered exponents and prove independence of chosen bases and uniformizer.
Define valuation and type by finite sums/counts; identify vertex and self-dual cases.
acceptance: Rank one with Gram π³ has val=3 and type=1; it is not a vertex lattice.
Invariants (0,1,1) give val=2, type=2 and a vertex lattice.
The cardinality of L∨/L is q^{2 val(L)} in an unramified quadratic extension, not q^{val(L)}.

nodes.title: LLL shortest-vector approximation bound
nodes.statement: For n≥1 and an LLL-reduced basis b of a full real Euclidean Z-lattice L, every nonzero x∈L satisfies ‖b₀‖²≤2^{n−1}‖x‖². Equivalently b₀ is within factor 2^{(n−1)/2} of the shortest nonzero vector.
hypotheses: L-membership is in the exact integer span of b, not the real span.
This is an approximation bound; it does not assert exact SVP or CVP.
proofSteps: Expand x with integer coordinates and choose its largest nonzero coordinate index k. Its absolute coefficient is at least one.
Project to b*_k to obtain ‖x‖²≥‖b*_k‖².
Apply the reduced orthogonal-length growth bound from k to the first vector and enlarge 2^k to 2^{n−1}.
acceptance: For n=1 the factor is 1 and the basis vector is shortest.
Replacing integer coordinates by real coefficients destroys the lower bound on the last nonzero coefficient.

proofSteps: Separate the empty-generic branch using empty-generic-density-zero; the nonempty branch retains its dimension and Hironaka/Gan–Yu existence gap.

nodes.title: Strong duality on a category
nodes.statement: A strong duality on a category C is a functor D:Cᵒᵖ→C and a natural isomorphism η:Id_C→D D with D(η_X)∘η_{DX}=id_{DX}. This is classical categorical duality, distinct from a stable Poincaré infinity-category.
hypotheses: C uses its existing category structure; opposite functors have the pinned map direction.
Exactness and additivity are extra properties, not empty proposition fields standing in for them.
proofSteps: Use the native opposite category, functor and natural isomorphism.
State and retain the double-dual coherence equation.
Use coherence and η to recover the contravariant equivalence; do not replace the category by an untyped involution on objects.
acceptance: Identity double-dual data on a discrete one-object category is a strong duality.
The functor reverses morphism composition.
A natural transformation that is not invertible gives the source’s weak duality, not this strong-duality structure.

nodes.title: Quaternionic integral hermitian lattices
nodes.statement: An embedded full central-ring lattice L in a right quaternion module is stable under the chosen star-stable quaternion order O. A nondegenerate pairing h has h(xa,yb)=star(a)h(x,y)b and h(y,x)=star(h(x,y)); integrality means h(L,L)⊂O. The right module is represented by the native opposite-ring action and the quaternion algebra and standard involution by an actual algebra-isomorphism model.
hypotheses: Characteristic-zero central fraction field, standard-involution quaternion algebra, order full over the central ring, and a right module whose opposite-ring action is compatible with central scalar multiplication. The pairing is perfect on the generic space; integral regularity is an additional condition.
proofSteps: Import B and its standard involution and reuse the native full finite R-submodule.
Add actual right O-stability and the noncommutative sesquilinear pairing conditions.
Localize the order, lattice and pairing together and compare only within those fixed local orders. The order/module localization and source-specific quaternionic classification remain named gaps.

Taking reduced trace of H(1,1)=1 gives 2, so reduced-trace metric normalization is a separate comparison.
Changing the order changes the integral-isometry problem even when the ambient quaternion algebra is unchanged.

Record the two alternatives and transport them along integral isometry.
Keep the binary dyadic alternative distinct from field diagonalization.

nodes.title: Adelic weighted mass identity
nodes.statement: Let q be totally positive over a totally real number field, G=SO(q), and K_f the integral stabilizer of a fixed lattice in its finite adelic genus. For compatible product Haar measures with convergent product vol(K_f), proper mass equals vol(G(K)\G(A))/(vol(G(K∞))·vol(K_f)). Every double-coset contribution is the reciprocal order of the proper integral stabilizer.
hypotheses: Use proper SO classes and weights consistently.
Local measures, archimedean measure and the convergent product are fixed before numerical evaluation.
The numerator is not replaced by 2 until a separate Tamagawa-number theorem is supplied; low-rank tori have separate behavior.
proofSteps: Identify proper genus classes with G(K)\G(A_f)/K_f.
Decompose the adelic quotient over these finitely many double cosets.
Integrate each compact archimedean/stabilizer piece, dividing by its finite rational stabilizer.
Sum the contributions and divide by the actual positive local-volume product; the Tamagawa comparison and explicit densities remain precise gaps.
acceptance: Rescaling one local Haar measure changes the numerator and local factor compatibly.
For proper rank-one classes the SO stabilizer is trivial and mass equals class count. A proper class whose stabilizer has order four contributes 1/4; for example SO(Z^2,x^2+y^2) has order four.
The numerical constant 2 is not an assumption-free formula for SO of rank 1 or 2.

nodes.title: Davenport semialgebraic multiset estimate
nodes.statement: For n≥1, a bounded semialgebraic multiset R⊂R^n with maximum multiplicity m, given by at most k polynomial inequalities of degrees≤ell, and an upper or lower triangular unipotent image R′, the multiplicity-weighted integer count differs from vol(R) by at most C(n,m,k,ell)·max(1,max_{1≤d<n}vol_d(proj_d R)). Projections are coordinate projections of the original region R.
hypotheses: The n=1 inner projection maximum is empty and the error bound uses 1.
The complexity and multiplicity control the uniform constant; boundedness alone is not enough.
General linear transformations are not silently treated as the triangular-unipotent variant.
proofSteps: Prove the coordinate-line interval bound for the region and every coordinate projection.
Iterate one-dimensional count/length comparisons to reduce to projection volumes.
For semialgebraic regions, use the corrected algebraic-cell argument rather than the false claim that every projection is a basic conjunction of polynomial inequalities.
The original Davenport proof, 1964 corrigendum and Rogers bounded-cell proof must be acquired and decomposed; only the precise modern statement is read.
acceptance: For an interval [0,N] with N integral, count−length=1.
Counting a region twice multiplies both volume and point count; ignoring multiset multiplicity is wrong.
The projection error for a triangular image refers to the original region as in Proposition 2.5.

nodes.title: Howe–Moore matrix-coefficient decay
nodes.statement: For a connected noncompact almost-simple real Lie group G with finite centre and a strongly continuous unitary representation on a Hilbert space with no nonzero G-invariant vector, every matrix coefficient tends to 0 as g leaves all compact subsets of G.

For a semisimple product one must specify escape in every noncompact factor or the appropriate factor-invariant exclusions.
proofSteps: Apply the exact Howe–Moore unitary-representation theorem, keeping its group and invariant-vector hypotheses.
For homogeneous quotient applications, construct the unitary action on the zero-mean L² subspace.
The full decay proof and the L² continuity/unitarity adapter remain explicit inputs.
acceptance: A constant vector in the full L² quotient space has a nondecaying coefficient; remove constants before applying the theorem.

nodes.title: Ergodicity of a noncompact subgroup action

hypotheses: Finite quotient volume is used to normalize μ; G is almost-simple, not an arbitrary product.
proofSteps: Construct the strongly continuous unitary action on zero-mean L²(G/Γ,μ).
If an H-invariant vector existed, its matrix coefficient would stay constant along an H-sequence leaving compact sets.
Apply Howe–Moore to force that vector to vanish and use the L² characterization of ergodicity.

nodes.title: Dani–Margulis recurrence in the lattice space
nodes.statement: For d≥2, X=SL_d(R)/SL_d(Z), a one-parameter unipotent subgroup u_t, x∈X and epsilon>0, there exists a compact K⊂X such that for every T>0, Leb{t∈[0,T]:u_t x∈K}/T≥1−epsilon.

proofSteps: Use Mahler compactness to describe cusp escape by short lattice vectors.
Apply the original Dani–Margulis polynomial/unipotent nondivergence estimate to construct K.
The estimate and its finite-interval uniformity are explicit proof acquisition gaps.

nodes.title: Ratner orbit-closure theorem
nodes.statement: For a connected linear semisimple real Lie group G, a lattice Γ, a connected subgroup U generated by one-parameter unipotent subgroups and x=gΓ, the closure of Ux is Lx for a connected closed subgroup L containing U, with L∩gΓg^−1 a lattice in L.

A general diagonal orbit does not satisfy this conclusion.

nodes.title: Margulis’s theorem on irrational quadratic values
nodes.statement: For n≥3, a real nondegenerate indefinite quadratic form q on R^n that is not proportional to a form with rational coefficients has q(Z^n) dense in R.
hypotheses: Nondegeneracy, indefiniteness, dimension≥3 and irrationality up to scalar are all retained.
proofSteps: For n=3 use G=SL_3(R) and H=SO(q)° generated by unipotents.
Use Ratner orbit closure and the H-to-G intermediate subgroup classification.
A closed finite-volume H-orbit forces a rational defining form by Borel density, contradicting the scalar-irrationality assumption.
The dense orbit then gives dense quadratic values by continuity and q(R³)=R. The intermediate subgroup, rationality and higher-dimensional restriction arguments are precise gaps.
acceptance: An integral form has discrete values and is excluded.
Positive-definite forms do not have values dense in all R.
The n=2 form x²−(3+2√2)y² shows why dimension≥3 is required.

nodes.title: Duke spherical lattice-point equidistribution
nodes.statement: As n→∞ through positive square-free integers n not congruent to 7 modulo 8, the normalized counting measure on {v/√n:v∈Z³,‖v‖²=n} converges to normalized rotation-invariant surface measure on S².

nodes.title: Polar-body transference lower inequality
nodes.statement: For a full real Euclidean lattice L and symmetric convex body K with nonempty interior, λ_i(K,L)·λ_{n+1−i}(K°,L*)≥1 for 1≤i≤n, where K° is the inner-product polar and L* the pairing-integral dual.
hypotheses: Use the same inner-product and intrinsic dimension on both sides.
The sharp upper transference and covering bounds require separate source theorems; they are not exported by this elementary lower bound.
proofSteps: Choose attained independent families at the two indicated minima.
The two spans have dimensions summing to n+1, so the dual family cannot pair to zero with the entire primal span.
A nonzero integral pairing has absolute value at least 1; the polar inequality bounds it above by the product of the two minima.
acceptance: For L=Z^n and K=product_i[-a_i,a_i], a_i>0, the polar is the cross-polytope sum_i a_i|y_i|<=1. The ordered minima of K are sorted reciprocals 1/a_i and those of its polar are sorted a_i, so the oppositely indexed products equal one.
An arbitrary real pairing has no integer ≥1 floor.

nodes.title: Mahler compactness criterion

proofSteps: Use a reduced-basis bound from successive minima and fixed covolume to obtain uniformly bounded representative bases.
Extract a convergent matrix subsequence; determinant 1 prevents rank collapse.
The converse follows from continuity and positivity of the shortest-vector function. Source proof-local reduced-basis/quotient-topology adapters remain gaps.

A nonclosed subset with a uniform first-minimum bound is relatively compact, but need not be compact.

nodes.title: Mass formula for maximal integral lattices
nodes.statement: Let K be totally real of degree d≥2, Q a totally positive nondegenerate m-dimensional form, m≥3, and Λ the genus of maximal integral O_K-lattices. With ordinary O-isometry mass, r=floor(m/2), G=SO(Q), 2 mass(Λ)=2 γ_G^d |disc K|^(dim G/2) L(G) ∏_p λ_p(Q). Here dim G=r(2r−(−1)^m); γ_G=∏_(i=1)^r(2i−1)!/(2π)^(r(r+1)) for odd m and (r−1)!∏_(i=1)^(r−1)(2i−1)!/(2π)^(r²) for even m. L(G)=∏_(i=1)^r ζ_K(2i) for odd m; ζ_K(r)∏_(i=1)^(r−1)ζ_K(2i) for even m with square discriminant; otherwise [ζ_E(r)/ζ_K(r)] N(d_E/K)^(r−1/2)∏_(i=1)^(r−1)ζ_K(2i), E=K(√disc Q). The local λ_p are exactly the table in Definition 3.1, not the hermitian normalized density polynomial of GN.3.
hypotheses: Maximal integrality is essential. Do not apply this formula to arbitrary lattices or indefinite forms.
The leading two multiplies the ordinary O mass; τ(SO)=2 has a separate original-source proof obligation.
The finite exceptional product and convergent positive-integer zeta Euler products are required.
proofSteps: Import rational field invariants and local classification from their existing owners.
Use the maximal-lattice single-genus result and local-type table.
Apply the Shimura/Gan–Hanke–Yu mass theorem with its archimedean and Tamagawa normalizations.
Separate the ordinary O mass from the proper SO adelic measure identity; identify every local factor, including dyadic places.
acceptance: Class number one implies mass=1/|Aut L|; it is not an unweighted class count.
The formula is restricted to m≥3; binary zeta-at-one substitution is excluded.
A dyadic exceptional factor is retained rather than set to one.

nodes.title: Eventually empty integral representation counts
nodes.statement: For complete discrete valuation fields in the stated unramified hermitian setting, if the generic representation scheme Rep(M,L)(F0) is empty, there is N0 such that every integral Gram representation count modulo pi^N is zero for N>=N0. Consequently every fixed-power normalized count is eventually zero and its limit is zero.
hypotheses: The unramified analytic density branch allows residue characteristic 2; geometric §3.4 hypotheses are not imported into all of §3.
Haar measures on lattice coordinates assign volume 1 to the integral coordinate lattice before any self-dual Fourier normalization is applied.
proofSteps: In fixed integral bases let C_N be the matrices in the compact integral coordinate lattice whose Gram equations hold modulo pi^N.
Each C_N is closed, C_(N+1) is contained in C_N, and the intersection consists exactly of integral Gram solutions.
A solution over the integral ring would extend to a generic representation, so the intersection is empty. The compact finite-intersection property gives some empty C_N0.
Every finite quotient matrix lifts to integral coordinates. Thus emptiness of C_N0 and all subsequent C_N forces eventual zero counts.
acceptance: For a rank-one target of norm 1 and source of norm pi, reduction modulo pi has a zero-vector solution, while modulo pi^2 no solution can have norm of valuation one. Generic emptiness implies eventual zero, not zero at every finite level.

nodes.title: Odd local signed Witt comparison
nodes.statement: The exact-category Witt quotient for finite signed-hermitian vector spaces identifies with the anisotropic-class Witt group. For a quadratic extension it has order four, C2×C2 when −1 is a norm and C4 otherwise. The trivial-extension alternating case is zero; the orthogonal case imports the existing field Witt theory.
hypotheses: Nonarchimedean local fields of odd residue characteristic; commutative trivial or quadratic extension with its specified involution.
proofSteps: Use the perfect duality induced by the field involution and sign on finite vector spaces.
Witt decomposition identifies quotient classes with anisotropic kernels; rank-one norm classes give the stated finite group.
acceptance: The conclusion retains every stated hypothesis and normalization.

nodes.title: Signed hermitian transfer
nodes.statement: For finite E/F with extending involutions and a nonzero involution-equivariant F-linear map λ:E→F, restriction of scalars with λ∘h gives a perfect ε-hermitian form. It sends a hyperbolic E-plane to [E:F] hyperbolic F-planes and induces a Witt homomorphism.
hypotheses: Nonarchimedean local fields of odd residue characteristic; commutative trivial or quadratic extension with its specified involution.
proofSteps: Nonzero λ and field multiplication make the transferred radical zero.
A maximal isotropic subspace has the required half-dimension after scalar restriction.
Use the hyperbolic relation to descend; the trivial-involution quadratic case is the supplier transfer.
acceptance: E=F and λ=id give the identity.
A hyperbolic plane transfers to degree-many hyperbolic planes.
The zero linear functional on a positive-rank space is degenerate and is excluded.

scope: Physical pp.1–8 visually read in full: introduction and §1 through termination and the statement of Proposition 1.26; complexity proof on p.9 and polynomial factoring sections not read.

Physical pp.157–168 / printed pp.137–148: §9.3–9.8, including full local-global lattice proofs and completion descent; the normalized-form proof cites an external algorithm, recorded as a gap. No whole-book reading or publisher collation is claimed.

Physical pp.2–4, 8–9, 14–19, 20–24 read: intro hypotheses; §1.7 hermitian lattices and measure normalization; §3 representation densities, normalized polynomial and Cho–Yamauchi formula including the p.18 proof. Geometric intersection sections are contextual reading, not mathematical claims owned by GN. Hironaka, Cho–Yamauchi, Kitaoka and Gan–Yu proofs cited by §3 were not acquired.

Physical pp.1–19 / printed pp.105–123: exact duality, symmetric spaces, Lagrangians, isotropic reduction, degree-zero GW/W, form functors, hermitian Q, GW space, formations and degree-zero comparison, with selected proofs in full. Physical pp.36–37 / printed 140–141: s-filtering conditions, exact quotient and localization statement; the remaining localization proof is not read.

Physical p.55, pp.57–58, and tail of p.56 read: cone swindle, filtering consequence, hermitian suspension, delooping and nonconnective Ω-spectrum warning. Full §9.1 cone setup and §5 cofinality proof not read.

Physical pp.1–4 introduction read: uniquely 2-divisible mapping-complex hypothesis, derived invariance, Bott triangle and shifted rather than homotopy-degree periodicity. Full §6 proofs remain precise gaps.

Physical pp.1–8 read: introduction and Recollection R.1–R.5. Physical pp.49–57 read: §3.1 homotopy-limit results and proofs; §3.2 symmetric/symplectic integral groups and their proof, duality action and low-degree table. Generic stable Poincaré/flavour theory belongs to the routed HermitianKTheoryOfPoincareCategories owner, not a second GN definition.

Physical pp.36–40 read in full: linking duality, canonical residue dualizing line, Corollary 2.2.5, ramified-uniformizer warning and symmetric-only dyadic devissage. The p.41 continuation of the explicit residue-boundary proof was not read.
Physical p.14 in full: Proposition 2.5 bounded semialgebraic multiset estimate and triangular-unipotent variant; its Davenport/Rogers proof inputs have not been acquired. No whole-paper claim.

Physical pp.1–3 / printed pp.73–75 read in full: spherical lattice-point application, theta/Weyl sum identity, square-free restrictions and Theorem 1. Full analytic coefficient proof and §§3–6 not read.

Physical pp.1–7 and19–21 read: actual quotient measure/lattice conventions, Mahler statement, Howe–Moore and Dani–Margulis recurrence statements, closed semisimple orbit finite-volume proof. Original mixing/recurrence proofs are cited but omitted by these notes, so remain gaps.

First page and physical p.59 / printed p.43 standing hypotheses; physical pp.412–415 / printed pp.396–399 reduction-theory context; physical pp.420–423 and426–429 / printed pp.404–407,410–413: Ratner orbit/measure/equidistribution statements and Margulis quadratic-value proof for three variables. Full Ratner proofs, higher-dimensional Oppenheim reduction and the rest of the book not read.

Physical pp.1–2 read in full: Theorem 1 and Remark 1, covering radius, cubic-lattice example and Claim 3 proof. Theorem 4 is stated with the weaker constant n; its pp.3–6 proof and the original 1993 proof were not read.

Physical pp.1–2 read in full: actual Euclidean dual/radius conventions and Theorems 1.1–1.2. The asymptotic improved constant is not exported as a uniform finite-dimensional bound; pp.3–6 proof not read.

Physical pp.1–5 read in full: integral/maximal lattice and genus definitions, local-type table, local mass factor table, Theorem 3.3 and beginning of Proposition 3.4 proof. Original Shimura/Gan–Hanke–Yu mass proof not acquired; remainder of classification not read.

checked.note: The coordinate Gram identity gives the squared norm of the alternating volume; complex conjugation and the real absolute square are retained.
Column norms in orthonormal coordinates give the determinant bound; the coordinate map is an isometry and does not change normalization.
The complex Gram determinant is nonnegative real and bounded by the product of squared norms; the prototype uses conjugate transpose rather than transpose.
A common norm bound is raised to twice the number of vectors; dependent vectors give determinant zero and need no inverse Gram matrix.
Covolume is taken in the lattice's real span, so its square equals the Gram determinant even when the ambient dimension is larger.
Monotonicity of the ordered positive quantities compares a tail product with the corresponding full product power; no arithmetic norm floor is assumed.
The positive-root inequality follows from the ordered tail product and a separately supplied lower norm bound, not from an arbitrary lattice.
The orthonormal coordinate map preserves Euclidean Haar measure, giving the product of side lengths without an extra Jacobian.
Coordinate bounds imply the Euclidean norm bound with the stated square-root dimension factor; zero dimension is separately normalized.
The cube inclusion supplies a dimension-dependent lower volume bound inside the intrinsic real span, with rank-zero Dirac volume handled separately.
Primitivity is the torsion-free quotient condition required to extend the subgroup basis; finite index without saturation would not suffice.
Projecting complementary adapted columns gives the quotient lattice basis; projection is injective only on the complementary real span.
Block triangular orthonormal coordinates give a product of Gram determinants; using squared determinants avoids the source's orientation slip.
The dual-basis Gram matrix is the inverse primal Gram matrix; nonsingularity follows from independence in the lattice span.
Pairing with a projected vector equals pairing with its original vector for a vector in the orthogonal complement; this proves the dual membership identity.
The integral orthogonal intersection is primitive; its rank is the complementary dimension, and the source's incorrect projected-column label is avoided.
The adapted Gram product yields the covolume quotient with positive square roots; arbitrary signed block determinants are not identified with covolumes.
Inverse Gram determinants yield reciprocal covolumes in the same real span and with the same Euclidean measure.
Projection duality and ambient unimodularity yield equality for a primitive integral sublattice; nonsaturated subgroups are excluded.
The finite-rank gauge infimum uses nonzero interior and full discrete lattices; the prototype explicitly distinguishes definition from attained witnesses.
A positive gauge sublevel is compact and its lattice intersection finite; compact convex bodies alone do not ensure absorbing gauges.
Finiteness below a fixed witness and positivity give a least gauge outside a proper subspace; the existence of that witness uses lattice span.
Choosing a least vector outside each preceding span gives independent vectors with nondecreasing gauges; no simultaneous minimum choice is presumed.
The greedy rank comparison identifies each attained gauge with the infimum definition, using spanning dimension rather than basis membership alone.
A sufficiently small neighborhood of zero contains no nonzero lattice point; attainment then makes each positive-rank minimum strictly positive.
The admissible rank requirements are nested, so successive minima are nondecreasing; zero-based indexing stays within the positive-rank range.
Attained independent vectors prove the non-strict threshold characterization; an infimum argument alone would only give a strict approximation.
The greedy family supplies independent vectors simultaneously at their respective minima, including the source's exact non-strict inequalities.
Enlarging the body enlarges each admissible set and decreases its gauge minima; both bodies retain the absorbing/interior hypotheses.
A lattice inclusion enlarges the set of candidate vectors, with the common span and full-rank assumptions needed to compare indices.
Positive body dilation rescales the gauge by its reciprocal; the zero scalar is excluded and the unchanged lattice is explicit.
The source's earlier invertibility convention agrees with LinearEquiv; both lattice and body are transported. The E11 error attribution is removed.
The first minimum is the least positive gauge of a nonzero lattice vector, with compact-discrete attainment supplying the witness.
The simplex decomposition yields the factorial denominator and product of axis lengths; this is a crosspolytope, not a coordinate box.
Convex symmetry and the attained independent minimum vectors place the weighted crosspolytope inside the body.
An independent lattice family spans a finite-index sublattice; its determinant is at least the full lattice covolume, with the index convention checked.
The crosspolytope volume and sublattice covolume comparison give the sharp 2^n/n! lower product constant.
The diagonal lattice/box example gives each coordinate threshold in the stated order and distinguishes scaling from polar-box conventions.
The independent coordinate axes attain the crosspolytope thresholds and the product saturates the lower Minkowski constant.
An invertible coefficient map changes box volume by the absolute determinant; a singular system would not have this finite-volume preimage.
The imported first Minkowski theorem applied to the linear-form box retains its determinant and strict/non-strict volume hypotheses.
Two points in a convex symmetric body have half their difference in that body; this is the geometric input to a finite coset injection.
Henk Lemma 2.1 bounds lattice points by the finite quotient index when the difference subgroup avoids the dilated body; the subgroup and avoidance hypotheses are retained.
Equal residue classes would produce the forbidden nonzero difference, so the point set injects into the finite quotient; infinity is not encoded as index zero.
Scaling beyond the first minimum prevents nonzero sublattice points in the required doubled body, with the strict inequality matching the residue argument.
Uniform integer dilation gives the non-strict rank-one-compatible count; this is kept distinct from Henk's strict higher-dimensional product bound.
